content.text: Teacher feedback anchors the comparison. Razmi and Ghane (2024) reported that Iranian male learners receiving WCF outperformed controls on writing performance and self-efficacy and showed lower writing anxiety, though the sample was small, exclusively male, and intermediate-level. Zhang and Hyland (2018) showed that teacher feedback addressed more error types than automated writing evaluation (AWE), which tended to highlight rather than correct errors; the highly engaged learner outperformed the moderately engaged one in responding to both sources. Learner preferences converge on explicit teacher input: university ESL students favoured direct correction combined with metalinguistic explanations over direct correction alone (Liu & Wu, 2019).

content.text: Experimental work indicates that feedback explicitness shapes accuracy gains and processing effort. Self-reported cognitive load was lower after direct corrections on grammatical errors than after metalinguistic codes on all errors (Bonilla López et al., 2018). Peer-mediated revision also produced meaningful score gains, although students ignored some peer comments (Li & Hebert, 2023). In an integrated approach, most students actively engaged and revised thoughtfully (Zhang and Hyland, 2021).
